facts.claim: Solya wrote "Tell Me It's Over" (writer and composer credit: Solya Lowe), and the song runs 2:56.
Danny Reisch produced the track, which is track 4 on the album Queen of Texas.
It was released on January 7, 2026 on VERSION III as the lead single from her debut album Queen of Texas. The album was announced the same day and came out March 6, 2026.

Solya wrote every track on the album and played rhythm guitar, synthesizers and piano. Producer Danny Reisch (Khruangbin, Local Natives) added percussion, and Jason Chronis (Tele Novella, Voxtrot) played bass and lead guitar.
The album was recorded on analog equipment over 10 days in Lockhart, Texas, after she wrote 10 songs following her first tour.
Solya said the feeling of the song was inspired by the 1950s and 60s, that its time signature feels very 50s, that she wanted it to sound raw, and that it was recorded on completely analog equipment.
Solya said she wrote the song after a breakup. She wasn't sad but angry, both at the pain the person caused her and at herself for not leaving sooner.
Press describe the song as a slow-burning, guitar-led track about the anger and clarity of leaving a toxic relationship, with Southern gothic-inspired production.

The album follows her independently released 2023 EP Fever Dream and 2024 EP Jewel Box, and early singles such as "Tear Me Apart" and "We Say Goodbye". Singles "Silver Swan", "Movie Star", "19" and "Born Wicked" came out in 2025 ahead of the album.

Solya Ava Lowe (born April 6, 2006) is a singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and producer from Abilene, Texas. She began releasing music independently in 2023 and signed with VERSION III in 2024.

research.lineage: The song sits in a Texas-rooted blend of Americana and dreamy indie rock with retro 1950s–60s pop melodies and twangy, analog-recorded textures.

draft:
The cruelest line in **Tell Me It's Over** is a request. "Tell me you never said I was the one," Solya sings, over and over, asking for a lie that would make leaving easier. If the promise was never made, nothing was broken, and nobody has to grieve it. The chorus turns a plea for closure into a command, repeated until it sounds less like asking and more like testing whether the words can be made true by saying them enough.

Solya has said she wrote the song after a breakup, and that she wasn't sad but angry, at the pain the other person caused and at herself for not leaving sooner. You can hear both angers in the lyric. The opening verse is defensive, bristling at being looked at like someone with "blood on my hands." Then comes the cool shot of pride: "You could've had it all." But the second verse lets the other feeling slip through. The narrator admits to searching for this person in every stranger they meet. Anger and longing sit right next to each other, and the song never pretends one cancels the other. The last new lines draw the boundary as plainly as possible: "And don't call me 'baby.'" It's a demand for distance from someone who still has the power to make a pet name hurt.

The music holds all of that at a slow, steady pace. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords with a slight tremolo shimmer. The bass sticks to simple root notes, and the drums keep a patient beat with the snare landing hard on two and four. The vocal is clear and a little breathy, sitting in the middle of the range, the notes held rather than pushed. There are no harmonies to soften it, just one voice in a clean, roomy mix with enough reverb to leave space around every sound.

That restraint is deliberate. Solya said she wanted the song to feel like the 1950s and '60s, with a time signature that feels very '50s, and to sound raw. That tremolo guitar and swaying beat are straight from the slow-dance ballad, bent toward the Southern gothic shade that press heard in Danny Reisch's production. The album was cut on analog equipment over ten days in Lockhart, Texas. Solya wrote it and played rhythm guitar, synthesizers and piano. Reisch, known for work with Khruangbin and Local Natives, added percussion, and Jason Chronis played bass and lead guitar. As the lead single from her debut, *Queen of Texas*, it lays out her approach clearly. It's old pop forms carrying very current fury.

The song works because it asks the other person to lie and keeps asking, and you feel how badly someone can want a clean ending they know they won't get.
